rows.etymology: 225. Kal. usuagín, usuagíṇḍ ‘afternoon, about 1:30-4 p.m.’ Trail and Cooper derive -gín, - gíṇḍ < OIA ghaṇṭā- ‘bell (stroke)’ (4421), which is not unlikely even though the lemma is not found independently in Kal. The first component usua- looks like Pk. visuva- ‘equinox’ – but which, I assume, is not the origin of the Kal. word – even though it fits semantically with OIA viṣuvánt- ‘midday, apex; Mitteltag, Scheitelpunkt’ (EWA) (MW gives viṣuva- ‘the shadow of the gnomon or index of a dial at noon when the sun is on the equinoctial points’) which is semantically somewhat different from CDIAL viṣuvánt, viṣuva- ‘equinox’. More promisising is comparison with Pr. vəs ‘day’ and the compound munǰesˈu ‘noon’ with munǰ- < OIA mádhya- ‘middle’. Pr. vəs ‘day’ has parallels in Kal. bas1 ‘day, 24 hours’, Ash., Wg. vās and Kt. vos all ‘day’. Turner derives the words < OIA vāsá- ‘abode, staying’ (11591), but this is implausible and in the NIA languages which are known to me in which this lemma is used it never means ‘day’ but always ‘overnight stay or place’. Therefore, Kal. usuagín, usuagíṇḍ may actually be a shortening of an expression originally having also started, like in Pr., with a reflex of OIA mádhya- ‘mid’ plus a *vas ‘day’ word. These words for ‘day’ are, I suggest, cognate with OIA *vasar- ‘morning’ (EWA [ii: 532]) which itself is cognate with VAS ‘shine, light up, get light (in the morning)’. Cf. also K. subas ‘prātaḥ – morning’ (Kaul [2006 ii: 398]), perhaps puilt after the borrowed word subah ‘morning’ from Ar.

rows.etymology: 1510. Deog. śuĩtāḷu ‘needle of a conifer’ is a synonym compound with first component < OIA *sūñcí̄- ‘needle’ (13551), a side-form of OIA sūcí̄-, and second component < OIA tú̄la- i.a. ‘pencil’ (5904) with vowel swapping. The word is interesting because Turner considers under lemma 13551 the possibility of OIA *śūcí̄-. This is supported by the Deog. form, OIA lex. v.l. śucĭ̄- (mentioned by Turner) and by Wg. šualá ‘tailor’ and šūṹ ‘to tailor’ (Z.). The palatal sibilants are either due to CCH, or, perhaps more plausibel, as argued by Turner, due to an original IA ś- because of Ash. arċú̄ċ ‘needle’ (with ar- < á̄rā- ‘shoemaker’s awl, driver’s hook’). Mayrhofer (EWA) agrees with this reconstruction and suggest that dental OIA s- is due to contamination by OIA s(y)ū- ‘to sew’. Since the contamination must have happened very early (the OIA word is attested from RV), the above forms with ś- clearly show that the contamination did not take place in all OIA dialects. There is also Kho. šūnǰ ‘needle’ which Morgenstierne (1936: 663) believes to be a borrowing from Iranian, and he therefore quotes Yid. šinǰo, šunǰ (< *šūžno which he compares with Mj. šižno). Close to these forms are Khot. suṃjsañu, Middle and New Pers. sōzan, Oss. sūʒīn, soʒīnæ all ‘needle’ and they in turn are close to dialectal OIA *śūñcí̄-. Note also the similarity, even though in an inverse order, of the synonym compounds Deog. śuĩtāḷu and Ash. arċú̄ċ. Turner quotes in addition a number of IA forms with affrication of the initial sibilant which he explains as assimilation of type of articulation, namely: Wg. čunċ, Dm. čũ̄či (quoted also above p. 326), dialectal Paš. čánčak, B. chũc, Or. chuñci, H. chũ̄chī. Pr. displays yet another variant of assimilation (namely in voice) in žim žižˈū ‘big needle (obsolete)’ with first word meaning ‘iron’ (OIA cīmara- ‘copper’ [14496]).

rows.etymology: 1520. Bng. śūr n.f. ‘a long and horizontal hole; a narrow path between the stone walls of fields, a hollow way’ and PAN ‘niche’; Deog. śūr ‘a hollow way’ (main meaning) but also ‘a burrow’, Kva. śūr ‘underground gallery’ — Jaṭ. sūrā ‘hole’ and in M.kuḍ. ‘holes in the shahanayi’ (wind instrument) < OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ (12570) with one modern (pre OIA) reflex in Wg. ċū ‘hole’. I add here also Kamd. ċˈüa- ‘bore a hole, make a hole’ (the form is found with Strand and the vowel is without nasalization). However, one finds the seemingly same Kamd. word ċyũ̄-stə ‘to bore’ (now Morgenstierne and vowel with nasalization) sub 12531a *śubati ‘bores’, where there is also a reference to Pers. sumb ‘hole’. The two unequal derivations nevertheless suggest an Indo-Iranian or even Indo-European origin of the Nuristan words. But this is questionable. Cheung (2007: 368) finds that the root *su(m)p/b¹ ‘to pierce, bore’ is only found in Iranian, a connection with OIA śvábhra- ‘gap, vault’ is very doubtful, and an Indo-European etymology cannot be found. However, there are a number of words for ‘hole’ in all three language groups which look similar enough to assume a common origin. It is, however, not so clear whether they can be connected with OIA *śūra-² or even with a PIE origin. Sub 12572 śūrtá- ‘crushed, broken’ Turner quotes Pal. ṣūṛ ‘hole, gullet’ but rightly assesses this as “very doubtful”. These are the words known to me: Pal. nasti-ṣó̄ṛa ‘nostril’; Ind. ṣùṛ ‘hole’ and ṣʌ́ō ‘a buttonhole’ (< older *ṣùō); Gau. nɑtẓó̄ᵃli ‘nostril(s)’; Dm. káᵃr-ṣui ‘ear-hole’, cf. also Pk. (Deś.) nakkasirā- ‘nostril’; Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ is probably a synonym compound with second component either < OIA kuṭa¹ ‘water-pot, pitcher’ (3227) or kāṭá-¹ ‘hole’ and can be compared with Brj. nakkua ‘nostril’; here probably related also the (apparent compound forms) Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’; Khaś. (Varma [1938: 53]) naśkuli, nakśuli, negśoi ‘nostril’; also here Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole; tiefes Loch’ (probably also a compound and borrowing from a Dardic language[?]), and Kal. ṣuṣuã́k ‘empty, hollow, dried up’ (apparently a reduplicated form and the meaning ‘dried up’ due to interference with Kal. ṣúṣu hik ‘to become dry’); Marm. ˈnʌkśuli and Deog. naksuṇi ‘nostril’ (with first syllable < OIA *nakka- ‘nose’ [6909]) (here we have again an example for an s – ś alternation), morphologically less clear are the similar sounding forms Kṭg. nəkthʊ́ṇi, nəkthóḷi, Kgr. nakthauṛi all ‘nostril’ (and Him. nakthró ‘bleeding from the nostril’?) with which, however, compare Bng. thūn ‘nostril’ (p. 813). Among the quoted forms are several without -ṛ, l, ṇ. Therefore it is likely that they are either some kinds of suffixes or represent the second components of compounds. Before discussing this question, I would suggest to derive Dardic ṣŭ̄ ‘hole’ < Proto-Dardic *šrŭ̄a- respectively *šrŭ̄ra- which derived < OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ through Dardic r-metathesis respectively r-spreading. Ind. ṣùṛ ‘hole’ and the other forms with the same flap consonant indeed seem to go back to a proto-form similar to the apparently unanalyzable Wg. ṣukˈuṛ (but see right below), and I want to suggest for them a proto-form šrŭ̄-puṭa-¹ ‘hollow cavity’, that is a synonym compound in typical Dardic fashion; this suggestion is supported by Paš.deg. naspar'ā ‘nostril’. The second component appears also in Nuristani and Dardic derivations of OIA nāsāpuṭa- ‘nostril’ (Pa.) (7090) (Nuristani and Dardic, e.g. Ash. nāsuṛi ‘nose’, but note also Ko. nākāčẽ puḍ ‘nostril’; the same kind of semantics is also found in M.kas. nakačɛ ḍɔlɔ ‘nostril’ < OIA *ḍalla-² ‘basket’ (5537).  Dardic ṣŭ̄ appears as a free form in old compounds (like Ind. ṣùṛ) and in compounds that cannot be so old like Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ and Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole’, both of which might contain as second element derivation < OIA kuṭa- 1 ‘water-pot, pitcher’ which is semantically similar to OIA puṭa-. Again a similar building pattern is found in Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’ with second element < OIA mūṭa- ‘basket’ (10233).  The above etymological interpretation of Dardic ṣŭ̄ allows a parallel analysis of the following words: Ind. ṣùl and Šaṭ. ṣúli ‘a nostril; a barrel; a tube for blowing at the fire; a spout; muzzle of a barrel’; Gau. ṣúlī ‘a tap’; Sh. ṣúlo and Bur. ṣúli ‘gun barrel, tube’; Wkh. ṣuli ‘chimney; pipe to get a flame’, all of which go back to a proto-form *šrŭ̄-nāḍí- ‘hollow tube’ (see OIA nāḍí̄- [7047]; because of the -l- the word might also be a borrowing, but see also Ind. nʌlkàʰ ‘a tube’). That the basic semantics for the above ‘nostril’ words is ‘nose-hole’ is supported by Bhaṭ. nɑ̈̃th̀ọr-sẹ sürè̄ʸ ‘nostrils’ (with -sẹ genitive postposition) which is a hybrid compound with the first component a Dardic word ‘nose’ and the last one a borrowing from Psht. sūrai ‘hole’. Regarding the origin of Psht. sūrai see Morgenstierne (1927: 69f.) who suggests to reconstruct *subra-ka- for Ydgh. surv and Wkh. sērv ‘hole’. Similarly, Cheung considers a Proto-Iranian reconstruction *subra- (ibid.). OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ is regarded to stand in a heteroclitic relationship to OIA śú̄na- ‘emptiness, lack, want, absence; ampty, bleak (öde)’ and derives < PIE *ḱóuhxr̥- ‘hole, opening’. A remarkable fact is that it is the Dardic meanings which fit pretty well e.g. with Greek kúar ‘eye of the needle, opening of the ear’ (cf. the many ‘nostril’ words above) whereas the West Pahāṛī words (‘hole; burrow’) fit quite well with Latin caverna ‘cave’. Note: There is also S. cur ‘cave’. Could this be a PIIr. archaism? Compare this with Nuristani Pr. kˈūču, kūč, kˈūči, kˈũču all ‘hole’ which, however, might be originally a synonym compound with first syllable reflecting OIA kú̄pa- ‘hole, hollow, cave’ (3400) and second syllable with loss of r as in Wg. ċū. In this case, the Prasun forms would be one more example of a non-dentalized reflex of a PIE palato-velar.

rows.etymology: 1520. Bng. śūr n.f. ‘a long and horizontal hole; a narrow path between the stone walls of fields, a hollow way’ and PAN ‘niche’; Deog. śūr ‘a hollow way’ (main meaning) but also ‘a burrow’, Kva. śūr ‘underground gallery’ — Jaṭ. sūrā ‘hole’ and in M.kuḍ. ‘holes in the shahanayi’ (wind instrument) < OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ (12570) with one modern (pre OIA) reflex in Wg. ċū ‘hole’. I add here also Kamd. ċˈüa- ‘bore a hole, make a hole’ (the form is found with Strand and the vowel is without nasalization). However, one finds the seemingly same Kamd. word ċyũ̄-stə ‘to bore’ (now Morgenstierne and vowel with nasalization) sub 12531a *śubati ‘bores’, where there is also a reference to Pers. sumb ‘hole’. The two unequal derivations nevertheless suggest an Indo-Iranian or even Indo-European origin of the Nuristan words. But this is questionable. Cheung (2007: 368) finds that the root *su(m)p/b¹ ‘to pierce, bore’ is only found in Iranian, a connection with OIA śvábhra- ‘gap, vault’ is very doubtful, and an Indo-European etymology cannot be found. However, there are a number of words for ‘hole’ in all three language groups which look similar enough to assume a common origin. It is, however, not so clear whether they can be connected with OIA *śūra-² or even with a PIE origin. Sub 12572 śūrtá- ‘crushed, broken’ Turner quotes Pal. ṣūṛ ‘hole, gullet’ but rightly assesses this as “very doubtful”. These are the words known to me: Pal. nasti-ṣó̄ṛa ‘nostril’; Ind. ṣùṛ ‘hole’ and ṣʌ́ō ‘a buttonhole’ (< older *ṣùō); Gau. nɑtẓó̄ᵃli ‘nostril(s)’; Dm. káᵃr-ṣui ‘ear-hole’, cf. also Pk. (Deś.) nakkasirā- ‘nostril’; Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ is probably a synonym compound with second component either < OIA kuṭa¹ ‘water-pot, pitcher’ (3227) or kāṭá-¹ ‘hole’ and can be compared with Brj. nakkua ‘nostril’; here probably related also the (apparent compound forms) Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’; Khaś. (Varma [1938: 53]) naśkuli, nakśuli, negśoi ‘nostril’; also here Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole; tiefes Loch’ (probably also a compound and borrowing from a Dardic language[?]), and Kal. ṣuṣuã́k ‘empty, hollow, dried up’ (apparently a reduplicated form and the meaning ‘dried up’ due to interference with Kal. ṣúṣu hik ‘to become dry’); Marm. ˈnʌkśuli and Deog. naksuṇi ‘nostril’ (with first syllable < OIA *nakka- ‘nose’ [6909]) (here we have again an example for an s – ś alternation), morphologically less clear are the similar sounding forms Kṭg. nəkthʊ́ṇi, nəkthóḷi, Kgr. nakthauṛi all ‘nostril’ (and Him. nakthró ‘bleeding from the nostril’?) with which, however, compare Bng. thūn ‘nostril’ (p. 813). Among the quoted forms are several without -ṛ, l, ṇ. Therefore it is likely that they are either some kinds of suffixes or represent the second components of compounds. Before discussing this question, I would suggest to derive Dardic ṣŭ̄ ‘hole’ < Proto-Dardic *šrŭ̄a- respectively *šrŭ̄ra- which derived < OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ through Dardic r-metathesis respectively r-spreading. Ind. ṣùṛ ‘hole’ and the other forms with the same flap consonant indeed seem to go back to a proto-form similar to the apparently unanalyzable Wg. ṣukˈuṛ (but see right below), and I want to suggest for them a proto-form šrŭ̄-puṭa-¹ ‘hollow cavity’, that is a synonym compound in typical Dardic fashion; this suggestion is supported by Paš.deg. naspar'ā ‘nostril’. The second component appears also in Nuristani and Dardic derivations of OIA nāsāpuṭa- ‘nostril’ (Pa.) (7090) (Nuristani and Dardic, e.g. Ash. nāsuṛi ‘nose’, but note also Ko. nākāčẽ puḍ ‘nostril’; the same kind of semantics is also found in M.kas. nakačɛ ḍɔlɔ ‘nostril’ < OIA *ḍalla-² ‘basket’ (5537).  Dardic ṣŭ̄ appears as a free form in old compounds (like Ind. ṣùṛ) and in compounds that cannot be so old like Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ and Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole’, both of which might contain as second element derivation < OIA kuṭa- 1 ‘water-pot, pitcher’ which is semantically similar to OIA puṭa-. Again a similar building pattern is found in Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’ with second element < OIA mūṭa- ‘basket’ (10233).  The above etymological interpretation of Dardic ṣŭ̄ allows a parallel analysis of the following words: Ind. ṣùl and Šaṭ. ṣúli ‘a nostril; a barrel; a tube for blowing at the fire; a spout; muzzle of a barrel’; Gau. ṣúlī ‘a tap’; Sh. ṣúlo and Bur. ṣúli ‘gun barrel, tube’; Wkh. ṣuli ‘chimney; pipe to get a flame’, all of which go back to a proto-form *šrŭ̄-nāḍí- ‘hollow tube’ (see OIA nāḍí̄- [7047]; because of the -l- the word might also be a borrowing, but see also Ind. nʌlkàʰ ‘a tube’). That the basic semantics for the above ‘nostril’ words is ‘nose-hole’ is supported by Bhaṭ. nɑ̈̃th̀ọr-sẹ sürè̄ʸ ‘nostrils’ (with -sẹ genitive postposition) which is a hybrid compound with the first component a Dardic word ‘nose’ and the last one a borrowing from Psht. sūrai ‘hole’. Regarding the origin of Psht. sūrai see Morgenstierne (1927: 69f.) who suggests to reconstruct *subra-ka- for Ydgh. surv and Wkh. sērv ‘hole’. Similarly, Cheung considers a Proto-Iranian reconstruction *subra- (ibid.). OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ is regarded to stand in a heteroclitic relationship to OIA śú̄na- ‘emptiness, lack, want, absence; ampty, bleak (öde)’ and derives < PIE *ḱóuhxr̥- ‘hole, opening’. A remarkable fact is that it is the Dardic meanings which fit pretty well e.g. with Greek kúar ‘eye of the needle, opening of the ear’ (cf. the many ‘nostril’ words above) whereas the West Pahāṛī words (‘hole; burrow’) fit quite well with Latin caverna ‘cave’. Note: There is also S. cur ‘cave’. Could this be a PIIr. archaism? Compare this with Nuristani Pr. kˈūču, kūč, kˈūči, kˈũču all ‘hole’ which, however, might be originally a synonym compound with first syllable reflecting OIA kú̄pa- ‘hole, hollow, cave’ (3400) and second syllable with loss of r as in Wg. ċū. In this case, the Prasun forms would be one more example of a non-dentalized reflex of a PIE palato-velar.

(Deś.) nakkasirā- ‘nostril’; Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ is probably a synonym compound with second component either < OIA kuṭa¹ ‘water-pot, pitcher’ (3227) or kāṭá-¹ ‘hole’ and can be compared with Brj. nakkua ‘nostril’; here probably related also the (apparent compound forms) Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’; Khaś. (Varma [1938: 53]) naśkuli, nakśuli, negśoi ‘nostril’; also here Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole; tiefes Loch’ (probably also a compound and borrowing from a Dardic language[?]), and Kal. ṣuṣuã́k ‘empty, hollow, dried up’ (apparently a reduplicated form and the meaning ‘dried up’ due to interference with Kal. ṣúṣu hik ‘to become dry’); Marm. ˈnʌkśuli and Deog. naksuṇi ‘nostril’ (with first syllable < OIA *nakka- ‘nose’ [6909]) (here we have again an example for an s – ś alternation), morphologically less clear are the similar sounding forms Kṭg. nəkthʊ́ṇi, nəkthóḷi, Kgr. nakthauṛi all ‘nostril’ (and Him. nakthró ‘bleeding from the nostril’?) with which, however, compare Bng. thūn ‘nostril’ (p. 813). Among the quoted forms are several without -ṛ, l, ṇ. Therefore it is likely that they are either some kinds of suffixes or represent the second components of compounds. Before discussing this question, I would suggest to derive Dardic ṣŭ̄ ‘hole’ < Proto-Dardic *šrŭ̄a- respectively *šrŭ̄ra- which derived < OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ through Dardic r-metathesis respectively r-spreading. Ind. ṣùṛ ‘hole’ and the other forms with the same flap consonant indeed seem to go back to a proto-form similar to the apparently unanalyzable Wg. ṣukˈuṛ (but see right below), and I want to suggest for them a proto-form šrŭ̄-puṭa-¹ ‘hollow cavity’, that is a synonym compound in typical Dardic fashion; this suggestion is supported by Paš.deg. naspar'ā ‘nostril’. The second component appears also in Nuristani and Dardic derivations of OIA nāsāpuṭa- ‘nostril’ (Pa.) (7090) (Nuristani and Dardic, e.g. Ash. nāsuṛi ‘nose’, but note also Ko. nākāčẽ puḍ ‘nostril’; the same kind of semantics is also found in M.kas. nakačɛ ḍɔlɔ ‘nostril’ < OIA *ḍalla-² ‘basket’ (5537).  Dardic ṣŭ̄ appears as a free form in old compounds (like Ind. ṣùṛ) and in compounds that cannot be so old like Ash. šukuṛə ‘hole of ear, nostril’ and Wg. ṣukˈuṛ ‘deep hole’, both of which might contain as second element derivation < OIA kuṭa- 1 ‘water-pot, pitcher’ which is semantically similar to OIA puṭa-. Again a similar building pattern is found in Klm. ṣumur H(L) ‘nose’ and Dara. ṣumūʔṛ ‘nose’ with second element < OIA mūṭa- ‘basket’ (10233).  The above etymological interpretation of Dardic ṣŭ̄ allows a parallel analysis of the following words: Ind. ṣùl and Šaṭ. ṣúli ‘a nostril; a barrel; a tube for blowing at the fire; a spout; muzzle of a barrel’; Gau. ṣúlī ‘a tap’; Sh. ṣúlo and Bur. ṣúli ‘gun barrel, tube’; Wkh. ṣuli ‘chimney; pipe to get a flame’, all of which go back to a proto-form *šrŭ̄-nāḍí- ‘hollow tube’ (see OIA nāḍí̄- [7047]; because of the -l- the word might also be a borrowing, but see also Ind. nʌlkàʰ ‘a tube’). That the basic semantics for the above ‘nostril’ words is ‘nose-hole’ is supported by Bhaṭ. nɑ̈̃th̀ọr-sẹ sürè̄ʸ ‘nostrils’ (with -sẹ genitive postposition) which is a hybrid compound with the first component a Dardic word ‘nose’ and the last one a borrowing from Psht. sūrai ‘hole’. Regarding the origin of Psht. sūrai see Morgenstierne (1927: 69f.) who suggests to reconstruct *subra-ka- for Ydgh. surv and Wkh. sērv ‘hole’. Similarly, Cheung considers a Proto-Iranian reconstruction *subra- (ibid.). OIA *śūra-² ‘hole’ is regarded to stand in a heteroclitic relationship to OIA śú̄na- ‘emptiness, lack, want, absence; ampty, bleak (öde)’ and derives < PIE *ḱóuhxr̥- ‘hole, opening’. A remarkable fact is that it is the Dardic meanings which fit pretty well e.g. with Greek kúar ‘eye of the needle, opening of the ear’ (cf. the many ‘nostril’ words above) whereas the West Pahāṛī words (‘hole; burrow’) fit quite well with Latin caverna ‘cave’. Note: There is also S. cur ‘cave’. Could this be a PIIr. archaism? Compare this with Nuristani Pr. kˈūču, kūč, kˈūči, kˈũču all ‘hole’ which, however, might be originally a synonym compound with first syllable reflecting OIA kú̄pa- ‘hole, hollow, cave’ (3400) and second syllable with loss of r as in Wg. ċū. In this case, the Prasun forms would be one more example of a non-dentalized reflex of a PIE palato-velar.

rows.etymology: 202. Bng. upsiṇɔ ‘to stretch o.s. and lounge around (after a heavy meal)’ < OIA *utpusati ‘swells’ (1828) (?) with parallels in Wg. and Kt. to which are to be added Chin. ubš ‘swelling’ and ubšbā ‘to swell’, Bashg. aps- ‘to be swollen’ and probably Wg. apsümřaṅdām ‘gut, colon; Darm, Dickdarm’ where Degener refers to a language consultant who says that initial aps- means ‘swell’. Turner suggests for some forms derivation < OIA *utpruṣati ‘bubbles up’ (1832) for Wg. and Kt. but his arguments for irregulat phonetic developments are not convincing. Therefore cf. possible reflexes of PIE *p(h)eu- ‘swell’ (discussed p. 659) and cf. Lat. pustula (Mallory and Adams [2006: 385]).
